title: Quiz: Market Basket Analysis and the Apriori Algorithm

questions.text: A transaction database has 200 transactions. The itemset {dental, vision} appears in 50 of them. What is supp({dental, vision})?
questions.explanation: Support = number of transactions containing the itemset / total transactions = 50 / 200 = 0.25. Support is always a proportion between 0 and 1.

questions.text: supp({dental}) = 0.40, supp({dental, vision}) = 0.30. What is conf(dental → vision)?
questions.explanation: conf(dental → vision) = supp({dental, vision}) / supp({dental}) = 0.30 / 0.40 = 0.75. This means that 75% of transactions containing dental also contain vision.

questions.text: A rule has confidence = 0.80 and supp({vision}) = 0.80. What is the lift of the rule X → vision?
questions.explanation: lift = conf / supp(consequent) = 0.80 / 0.80 = 1.00. Lift = 1 means X and vision are statistically independent — knowing X tells you nothing extra about vision beyond its base rate.

questions.text: The anti-monotone (Apriori) property states that if an itemset X is infrequent, then:
options: All subsets of X are also infrequent
All supersets of X are also infrequent
All rules derived from X have low confidence
X cannot appear as the consequent of any rule
questions.explanation: If supp(X) < min_supp, then for any superset Y ⊃ X, every transaction containing Y also contains X, so supp(Y) ≤ supp(X) < min_supp. This allows Apriori to prune all supersets of infrequent itemsets without scanning them.

questions.text: A rule with lift = 2.5 means the co-occurrence of X and Y is 2.5 times more frequent than if they were statistically independent.
questions.explanation: Lift = P(X ∩ Y) / (P(X) × P(Y)). If X and Y were independent, P(X ∩ Y) = P(X) × P(Y) and lift = 1. Lift = 2.5 means they co-occur 2.5 times as often as independence would predict.

questions.text: You run Apriori with min_supp = 0.05 and find 10,000 frequent itemsets. Why might you want to also set a minimum confidence threshold when generating rules?
options: Confidence filters out rules with low support
Without a confidence threshold, trivial rules like 'if A then A' are generated
High support alone does not guarantee a useful rule — confidence measures the conditional strength of the relationship
Confidence and support are identical metrics
questions.explanation: An itemset can be frequent (high support) but the rule X → Y might still have low confidence if Y is rarely present when X is. Confidence = P(Y|X) measures how reliably Y follows X, filtering out weak or unreliable associations.
